Angola wants to stop the spread of a cholera outbreak that has killed hundreds of people. Plus, reinventing Jacob Zuma: Can Africa's former deputy president salvage his political career? And the legacy of a man who brought help to Ethiopia is documented on film by his son. All this and more on INSIDE AFRICA.

Hello, I'm Isha Sesay. Welcome to INSIDE AFRICA, our weekly look at news and life on the continent. Contaminated water and inadequate sanitation are taking their toll in Angola. The country is working to contain an outbreak of cholera. More than 1,000 people have died, and more than 30,000 residents have contracted the disease. Officials report nearly 500 new cases of cholera each day. The humanitarian group Doctors Without Borders is on the ground in Luanda. Earlier, we spoke with the group's executive director, Nicolas de Torrente, about the scale of the outbreak.

speaker_label: NICOLAS DE TORRENTE, DOCTORS WITHOUT BORDERS
text: Well, this is a very large outbreak. Cholera has been endemic in Angola, and there have been outbreaks in the late '80s, early '90s, but Angola has not seen an outbreak of cholera since 1994. And so far, since February 13th, when the first case was detected in Luanda, there have been 33,000 cases reported in Luanda, the capital, but also spread around the country, with reported 1,200 deaths. We estimate probably that that -- that number is lower than the reality, because many deaths go unreported.
Those are huge numbers you -- you're giving us there. How do you account for this outbreak?

Well, there's been, you know, Luanda is a very big city now. It's 2.5 million people, and the vast majority of these people live in very, very poor living conditions, in shantytowns, where there is, you know, there is no running water. People get water from trucks. There is very poor sanitation conditions and no waste disposals, switch facilities. And this is really the perfect breeding ground, the recipe for disaster, really, when you have the beginning of an outbreak, and that has really fueled the epidemic.
Yet cholera is the disease that can be easily treated. So, how do you account for the number of lives that have been lost?

Well, you're right. Cholera, you know, cholera is a diarrheal disease, and what it's -- it's transmitted from person to person, oral/fecal contamination. And you know, when someone gets it, what happens is massive dehydration. And you know, people lose a lot of fluid within a matter of hours and can die very quickly. However, if you are able to bring them to a cholera treatment center quickly enough and able to simply rehydrate them, either through oral rehydration fluids or, if they're vomiting very much, through IV fluids, we're able to -- to treat them and they recover. We have less than 1 percent mortality rates in cholera treatment facilities, and we've expanded these very much, but there're still, you know, there's still a lot of cases that go on unreported, people come late, and, you know, at a certain point we were quite overwhelmed with the number of cases.
And according to the U.N. Children's Fund, children under five account for about 35 percent of cholera victims.

That's right. That's what we're seeing in Angola today. About 35 percent of the cases in our centers are children. The children are usually more vulnerable to -- to all sorts of illnesses, and cholera here is no exception. We're seeing, you know, in the last couple of days, we're seeing a slight decrease in -- in the number of cases reported in -- in -- Luanda, in the country, around the country. It's around 600 cases now per day in the country, half of them coming from Luanda. But it's really too early to tell whether, you know, we're starting -- we're starting to turn the corner on this epidemic. It's too early to tell whether the situation has stabilized, and a lot of efforts are still needed to contain this epidemic.
And give us some sense of the measures that are in place to try and contain this.

Well, treatment is, of course, the first thing for when people are already infected, to treat them and to save their lives, but more than that, you need to really deal with some of the immediate causes of the problem, which in particular are the water supply system. So our teams have been coordinating, for instance, one of the main collection points for -- the water tankers, who go into Luanda and give water in the poor neighborhoods, have been, you know, collect their water. We're coordinating that source. Authorities have started also to start now to deal with the water supply in the few of the worst hit areas. There's starting to be some mobilization around the immediate -- the containment measures are to prevent the further spread of the -- of the outbreak. But it's still far too little, and much more needs to be done.
Is there a public awareness campaign? I know that in the past, you've said your -- your organization has urged the Angolan government to do more. How is that working?

Yes. There is more -- there is more awareness now. We see that in the fact that people are coming to our centers earlier. We have done quite a massive effort in terms of going out to the community, doing outreach, explaining what the disease was, what measures could be taken, and trying to urge people to refer severe cases to -- to the treatment centers early. So that is, again, slowly starting to -- to pay off.

That was Doctors Without Borders' executive director, Nicolas de Torrente. Zuma stepped down from his role in the ANC after he was charged with rape, but the South African court found him not guilty, and some say his chances of becoming the country's next president aren't exactly finished.
